1.x: Matthew begins with three human titles for Jesus (Christ [anointed or Messiah- only humans are anointed], Son of David, Son of Abraham), and ends with three divine titles for Jesus (Son [God in His incarnation], Father [God as our creator], Holy Spirit [God in action] [Mt 28:19]). We see those three titles given to Jesus in Isaiah 9:6 as Son, Counselor (Spirit) and Eternal Father.

2.x: Abraham’s wife Sarah was barren for many years. In impatience, Sarah gives her servant Hagar to Abraham and they have a son, Ishmael (the father of Muslims). But God’s promise was specifically through Sarah(Gen 17:16,19,21). In their old age, Sarah miraculously gave birth to Isaac (Issac’s name means “laughter”, reflecting Sarah’s initial laughter in disbelief [Gen 18:12]). Abraham tried to sacrifice Isaac in obedience to God, foreshadowing the Father sacrificing the Son. Here, we already see a lack of a Trinity, (1) the Father (who is an invisible Holy Spirit) & (2) the Son (who is an authentic visible human being).

Who suffered more, the Spirit or the Flesh? The human Son nailed to the cross, or the Father whose love bore the weight of that sacrifice? As an omnipresent, infinite Spirit, the Father cannot experience physical nerve pain, yet Scripture reveals Him as deeply emotional, a "consuming fire" (Deut 4:24) whose heart can be "grieved" to its core (Gen 6:6). The Son, on the other hand, the authentic human temple in whom the fullness of God dwelt (Jn 2:19, Col 2:9), endured the full spectrum of human vulnerability. He experienced anguish so intense he sweated drops of blood (Lk 22:44), soul-crushing sorrow "even unto death" (Mt 26:38), and the agonizing torture of Calvary. While the flesh absorbed the physical blows, spikes, and asphyxiation, the indwelling Spirit of the Father bore the sorrow of laying the sin of the world upon His only begotten Son (Mt 1:20; Jn 3:16).

Isaac marries Rebekah, and has twin sons: Esau(older & hairy) & Jacob (younger & hairless). Jacob tricks Esau and steals his birthright and his blessing. Later, Jacob wrestles with God (or an angel) and his name is changed to Israel. Jacob marries two sisters: Leah & Rachel, & together became the fathers of Israel, for they begat the 12 sons that would lead the 12 tribes of Israel: (1) Reuben (firstborn to Leah, Jacob’s first wife), (2) Simeon (Leah), (3) Levi (Leah), (4) Judah (Leah), (5) Dan (Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant), (6) Naphtali (Bilhah), (7) Gad (Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant), (8) Asher (Zilpah), (9) Issachar (Leah), (10) Zebulun (Leah), (11) Joseph (Rachel, Jacob’s beloved wife), (12) Benjamin (Rachel, she died in childbirth).

3.x: “Judah,” ancestor of the tribe of Judah, from which King David and Jesus come. “Tamar” was Judah’s daughter-in-law, she married Judah’s firstborn son, Er (Gen 38:6-7). After Er died, the custom (levirate marriage) required the next brother to marry Tamar and produce offspring for the deceased brother. Judah told his second son, Onan, to do this. But Onan, knowing that the seed would not be his, refused to carry out his duty, so when he came unto Tamar, he spilled his semen on the ground instead. God “slew him” for that (Gen 38:8-10 KJV). Judah then promised his third son, Shelah, to Tamar, but never followed through. Instead, Tamar was left as a widow with no protection, no children, and no future. Seeing that Judah wasn’t going to keep his promise, Tamar acted boldly and disguised herself and approached Judah (who didn’t recognize her). Judah slept with her and she became pregnant. Tamar gave birth to twins: Perez (ancestor of King David & Jesus), and Zerah. Women are rarely listed in genealogies & her story is messy, however, Matthew probably added her to show how God works through imperfect people & imperfect situations. God’s plan isn’t hindered by human failure. “Perez” means “breaking through,” he unexpectedly came out first even though Zerah seemed first. The midwife had put a scarlet thread on Zerah’s hand as the firstborn, but later drew back his hand, and Perez “broke through” first. The “Perezites’ became a major clan in Israel (Num 26:20). “Hezron” (or Esrom) is listed among those who went down to Egypt during the time of Jacob (Gen 46:12). This places him at the beginning of Israel’s time in Egypt. “Ram” (Aram), his name varies, in OT genealogies, he appears as “Ram” (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chr 2:9-10) and in the NT, some mss have “Aram,” while others have “Ram” (Mt 1:3-4).

4.x: “Ram” in Hebrew means “high”, “exalted”, or “lifted up.” His name reflects elevation or prominence, although Scripture does not tell his story. “Amminadab” is Aaron’s (Moses’ brother) father-in-law; his daughter Elisheba married Aaron (Ex 6:23). “Nahshon” (or Naasson) is a significant figure during the Exodus. He is the leader of the tribe of Judah (Num 1:7). Jewish tradition says Nahshon was the first to step into the Red Sea before it parted. “Salmon” married Rahab (the woman who helped the Israelite spies in Jericho). His marriage links Israel with an outside, foreshadowing God’s inclusion of gentiles, as well as redemption & transformation.

5.x: “Rahab” is a Canaanite woman from Jericho who helped Israelite spies. She hid them & declared faith in Israel’s God (Joshua 2:9-11). She & her family were spared when Jericho fell. She is honored for her faith (Heb 11:31; Jms 2:25), even though she was a former outsider & prostitute. She is an example of faith over background & God’s mercy & inclusion of gentiles. “Boaz” (or Booz) is a wealthy & righteous man in Bethlehem. He shows kindness to a foreign widow: Ruth - purchases her, and marries her to raise up the name of her dead husband: “that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren” (Ruth 4:10 KJV). As a kinsman-redeemer, he foreshadows Jesus, redeeming others at personal cost. “Ruth” is a moabite woman (a foreigner) who chooses to stay with her mother-in-law Noemi, works humbly to survive, and marries Boaz & becomes part of Israel. She becomes the great-grandmother of King David. “Obed” is the son of Boaz & Ruth. After Obed is born, the women of Bethlehem say: “There is a son born to Naomi” (Ruth 4:17 KJV). Even though Ruth is the biological mother, the child is publicly associated with Naomi’s family line. This is due to the Levirate-like redemption (family line restoration), where if a man died without a son, a close relative would marry the widow, and the child would carry on the dead man’s name & inheritance (Deut 25:5-6). In Ruth’s case, Naomi’s son Mahlon (Ruth’s first husband) died. Boaz (a relative) marries Ruth and their child, Obed, legally continues Mahlon’s family line. Obed is the grandfather of King David. “Jesse” is the father of King David. Lived in Bethlehem and God chose his youngest son David to be king (1 Sam 16:11-13). Isaiah prophesied that the Messiah would be the “root of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:10 KJV).

6.x: “David” is Jesse’s youngest son (1 Sam 16:10-13). Though Jesse was not a king, he became the stem(trunk) from which the royal branch(line) came from (Isa 11:1,10). David is the 2nd King of Israel & the most important King of the OT. He was chosen by God (1 Sam 16:12-13). Defeats Goliath (1 Sam 17:23, 50). Becomes King (2 Sam 5:3). God establishes a covenant with him where his throne will be established forever (2 Sam 7:16). David means “Beloved”. He was a man after God’s heart (1 Sam 13:14). Jesus’ kingship is rooted in David’s line. The wife of Uriah is Bathsheba, with whom David commits adultery. Despite knowing she was married, David sent messengers to bring Bathsheba to the palace, slept with her & got her pregnant. David tried to cover up what he’d done, and summoned Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he would sleep with his wife & the pregnancy would appear to be Uriah’s. But Uriah refused. Out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers who were still camping in the open fields, he slept at the palace entrance with the servants instead of going home to his wife. David’s first plan failed, so he turned to something darker & wrote a letter to Joan (his army commander) & sent it with Uriah himself: ”Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire(withdraw) ye from him, that he be smitten, and die” (2 Sam 11:15 KJV). The prophet Nathan pronounced judgement on David: Violence would never depart from David’s house, someone close to David would take his wives in broad daylight (this later happened with Absalom), & the child born to Bathsheba would die on the seventh day (2 Sam 12:18). David repented and was forgiven, but he still had to suffer the consequences of his sin. By saying “wife of Uriah”, Matthew keeps attention on the wrong done & acknowledges Uriah (a faithful man). “Solomon,” another son of Bathsheba, is the 3rd King of Israel. Becomes King (1 Kings 1:39). Asks for wisdom (1 King 3:9-12). Builds the 1st temple (1 Kings 6:1-2). The name “Solomon” comes from shalom, meaning “peace”. His kingship was the golden age of Israel: 666 - wealth, wisdom, peace (1 Kings 10:14). But it ends in compromise as he falls into idolatry due to his women (1 Kings 11:4), showing how even a King after “God’s heart” & the wisest King fall short of the standard of God.

7.x: “Solomon” would make in one year 666 talents of gold (1 Kings 10:14), symbolizing the peak of Israel’s prosperity & Solomon’s glory as the richest & wisest King. Recall that 666 symbolizes the peak of humanity, which will also be the number of the beast in Revelation (Rev 13:18); only in God can we find completion in the number 7. Solomon’s wisdom made him popular, especially his decree on the two mothers & one baby (1 Kings 3:16-28). He’s the author of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, & Song of Songs. His life represents blessings plus the danger of success. His failure sets up the division of the kingdom - Wisdom without obedience still leads to downfall. “Rehoboam” is the first King of a divided kingdom. After Solomon dies, the people ask for lighter burdens (1 Kings 12:4). Rehoboam rejects wise counsel and answers harshly (1 Kings 12:13-14). The ten tribes rebel and the kingdom splits into Israel (north) & Judah (south, Rehoboam’s kingdom). Rehoboam means “he enlarges the people”, but instead of enlarging the people, he loses most of them. This shows that pride & poor leadership can destroy unity & that listening to bad advice can have massive consequences. “Abijah” (or Abia or Abijam) was also King of Judah. His name means “my father is YHWH”. His name honors God, but his life is spiritually inconsistent, as he walked in the sins of his father (1 Kings 15:3). “Asa” was one of the good kings of Judah. Removes idols and false worship (1 Kings 15:12). Even removes his grandmother from power for idolatry (1 Kings 15:13). He also trusts God in crisis - when faced by a massive army, he prayed to God & God gave him victory. However, later relies on a foreign alliance instead of God (2 Chr 16:7) & when he was sick from his feet, he relied on the physician instead of God (2 Chr 16:12), then died. Faithfulness must be maintained over time, not just started well. Leadership matters, one bad decision (Rehoboam) splits a nation. One faithful king (Asa) brings reform.

8.x: “Asa” was one of the most righteous kings of Judah, known for his early devotion to God & religious reforms. He removed idols and pagan altars from Judah. Even removed his grandmother Maacah from being queen because of her idolatry. However, later he relied on a treaty with Syria instead of trusting God (2 Chr 16:7) & trusted physicians instead of God (2 Chr 16:12). Had a strong start, but a compromised end. His son, “Jehoshaphat,” continued many of his father’s good reforms & strengthened Judah spiritually & politically. Sent teachers & Levites throughout Judah to teach the Law (2 Chr 17:7-9), removed any high places & Asherah poles (2 Chr 17:6) & established judicial reforms based on the fear of the LORD (2 Chr 19:5-7). In general, he was a godly king with notable faith, yet weakened by forming an alliance with the wicked King Ahab of Israel, for which he was rebuked by the prophet Jehu (2 Chr 19:2). “Joram” marks a sharp spiritual decline in the line of David. He married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab & Jezebel. Killed his own brothers to secure the throne, & led Judah into idolatry, following the ways of the house of Ahab. He received a letter from the prophet Elijah condemning his wickedness & God struck him with an incurable disease in his bowels. Died in great suffering, and “without being desired” (2 Chr 21:20 KJV). Matthew omits several kings between Joram & Uzziah (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah) in order to build a structured list of sets of 14, the number you get by adding the numerical value of each letter in the word “David.” “Uzziah” (or Ozias) was a powerful & successful king, especially early in his reign. However, “when he was strong, his heart was lifted up” (2 Chr 26:16 KJV), and he entered the temple unlawfully to burn incense (which was a Levite duty). So God struck him with leprosy & he lived isolated until death. He was a gifted & successful king whose pride led to downfall.

9.x: “Uzziah” (or Ozias) was one of Judah’s strongest kings - militarily, economically, and politically. He expanded Judah’s borders & subdued Philistines & Arabians. Built fortified towers in Jerusalem. Developed advanced war machines & strengthened agriculture. Sought God under the guidance of Zechariah. Prospered greatly as long as he sought the LORD. But when he became proud and unlawfully entered the temple to burn incense, he was struck with leprosy & lived in isolation until his death. A reign of strength undone by pride. “Jotham” (or Joatham) is a relatively quiet but consistently righteous king: “he prepared his ways before the LORD his God” (2 Ch 27:6 KJV). However, the people still acted corruptly - he did not fully remove high places. He was a steady & faithful ruler, though unable to fully reform the nation. “Ahaz” (or Achaz) represents a dramatic spiritual collapse in Judah’s leadership. He worshipped Ball & other idols. Practiced child sacrifice, promoted widespread idolatry throughout Judah. He faced invasion from Syria & Israel. Instead of trusting God, he appealed to Assyria for help. During his reign, Isaiah delivered the famous prophecy: “a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son” (Isa 7:14 KJV). In summary, he was a king of deep apostasy who led Judah into severe spiritual ruin. “Hezekiah” (or Ezekias) stands as one of Judah’s greatest & most faithful kings (in sharp contrast to his father). He reopened & cleansed the temple. Destroyed idols, including the bronze serpent (Nehushtan), which people had begun to “venerate” with incense (2 Kings 18:4). Restored proper worship & reinstituted Passover. He faced an invasion by Assyria, but he prayed to God & God miraculously delivered Jerusalem. 185,000 Assyrian soldiers were struck down in one night. He became mortally ill, prayed, & God extended his life by 15 years. One of his failures was to show Babylonian envoys all his treasures. This act led to the future Babylonian captivity. He was a godly reformer and man of faith, yet not without moments of pride and midjudgement.

10.x: “Hezekiah” (or Ezekias) was one of Judah’s most righteous kings, known for a revival & trust in God. He cleansed & reopened the temple. Restored Passover worship. Destroyed idols (including the bronze serpent). When Sennacherib invaded, Hezekiah prayed & God struck down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in one night. Became terminally ill, prayed, and God extended his life by 15 years. However, in his pride & vainglory, he showed off his wealth & military might to Babylonian envoys. Isaiah then confronted him & delivered God’s judgement: ”Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon…” (Isa 39:5-6 KJV). In summary, Hezekiah was a man of great faith, yet with a moment of pride that had long-term consequences. “Manasseh” (Manasses) is considered the most wicked king of Judah, yet also one of the greatest examples of repentance. He rebuilt high places his father destroyed. Worshipped Baal, stars, & pagan gods. Practiced sorcery & witchcraft. Placed idols inside the temple itself. Sacrificed his own son in fire. Shed “innocent blood very much” (2 Kings 21:16 KJV), and Jewish tradition holds that he persecuted prophets, possibly including Isaiah. However, taken captive by Assyria to Babylon with “a hook in his nose” (2 Chr 33:11 BSB), in affliction, he humbled himself greatly before God. God restored him to Jerusalem. After repentance, he removed idols, restored the altar of the LORD & commanded Judah to serve God. A life that plunged into the deepest sin, yet rose again through genuine repentance. “Amon” followed the early (wicked) ways of his father, but not his repentance. He continued with idolatry & corruption. “And humbled not himself before the LORD, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself” (2 Chr 33:23 KJV). At the end, he was assassinated by his own servants after only 2 years. The people killed the conspirators & made his son Josiah king. Amon has a brief & evil reign, marked by stubbornness & refusal to repent. “Josiah” (Josias) is one of Judah’s greatest reformers & a king of extraordinary devotion to God. He began seeking God at a young age (around 16). Started purging Judah of idols in his youth. During his reign, the Book of the Law was discovered in the temple (after being lost perhaps for 75 years = 55 years of Manasse’s wicked reign + 2 of Amon’s + 18 years that took Josiah to find it). When it was read, Josiah tore his clothes in repentance. He destroyed idols, altars, & pagan worship sites. Renewed covenant with God. Restored proper worship. Held one of the greatest Passover celebrations since the days of the judges. During his reign, prophets like Jeremiah & Zephaniah ministered. In his death, he went to battle against Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, and was killed at Megiddo. In summary, he was a deeply godly king whose reforms delayed judgement on Judah.

11.x: “Josiah” was a righteous reformer, but his death marked the beginning of Judah’s rapid collapse. Matthew says that Josiah “begat Jechonias and his brethren,” but this is not a direct father-son statement in the strict sense. There is a generational compression here (common in Jewish genealogies). Historically, Josiah’s sons were Johanan, Jehoiakim (Eliakim, but was renamed as Jehoiakim [2 Kings 23:34]), Zedekiah, and Shallum (1 Chr 3:15), who is generally identified with Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:30). And Jechonias (Jeconiah/Jehoiachin/Coniah) was actually Josiah’s grandson (son of Jehoiakim [2 Kings 24:6]). “Jechonias” (Jeconiah/Jehoiachin) reigned during the final crisis before the exile. He had a short reign, ruled only for about 3 months & 10 days. Did evil in the sight of the LORD. Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem. Jechonias surrendered & was taken captive to Babylon. He lived many years in Babylonian prison but was later released and given a pension. His short reign & deportation effectively ended the independent Davidic monarchy in Jerusalem. Matthew says “Jechonias and his brethren”, but this refers not to literal brothers only, but to the royal family / generation descending from Josiah - the last rulers of Judah before the full destruction of Jerusalem. They include (1) Jehoahaz (also called Shallum) - Josiah’s son, reigned only 3 months, deposed by Pharaoh & taken to Egypt, (2) Jehoiakim (Eliakim) - another son of Josiah, reigned 11 years, was evil, rebelled against Babylon, & died during the siege, and (3) Zedekiah - uncle of Jeconiah (another son of Josiah), installed as a puppet king by Babylon. He reigned 11 years, rebelled, leading to the final destruction of Jerusalem & temple in 586BC & the major exile. Matthew groups these last kings together as “Jeconiah & his brothers” to show the collapse of the monarchy “about the time they were carried away to Babylon” (KJV). People were taken into exile for ~70 years. This was God’s judgement due to persistent idolatry & covenant-breaking, specially the sins of Manasseh (2 Kings 24:3-4). Jeremiah warned of this judgement, Ezekiel ministered among the exiles, & Daniel lived in Babylonian courts.

12.x: “Jechoniah” (Jechonias) is cursed. In Jeremiah 22:30, God declares: “Write ye this man childless… no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David..” (KJV). The Messiah must come from David’s line, yet this line is seemingly cursed. This is resolved in three possible ways: (1) Christ was born through a virgin birth, or (2) this genealogical line is simply Jesus’ claim to the Davidic Kingdom through Joseph as his firstborn, but not his actual DNA lineage, which would come from Nathan instead of Solomon in Mary’s genealogy (Lk 3:31), or (3) God restores the Davidic line through Zerubbabel as his “signet ring” (Haggai 2:23 BSB), overwriting Jeconiah’s curse. “Shealtiel” (Salathiel) is Jeconiah’s son & heir of the royal line. He was born & lived in Babylon during the exile. Not much data is given about him in Scripture, but he represents the continuation of the Davidic line in exile. “Zerubbabel” (Zorobabel) was a central figure in the return from exile. Was the governor of Judah under Persian authority (Haggai 1:14) & led the first group of Jews returning from Babylon around 538BC after King Cyrus of Persia allowed it (Ezra 1:1-3). He rebuilt the Second Temple in Jerusalem as the “signet ring” of the LORD (Haggai 2:23 BSB). God had told Jeconiah that even if he were like a signet ring on God’s hand, He would pull it off & cast him away into exile (Jer 22:24). This symbolized the temporary removal of the Davidic line’s ruling power due to sin. Now, through Zerubbabel, God was restoring honor to the line - the covenant promises to David were not cancelled.

13.x: “Zerubabbel” brought many Jews back to Jerusalem under Persian King Cyrus (Ezra 2:2). Together with the high priest Joshua, he rebuilt the altar (Ezra 3:2) & laid the foundation for the Second Temple (Ezra 3:8). God called him a “signet ring” (Hag 2:23 BSB) - a symbol of restored honor & authority to the Davidic line after the judgement of exile. “Abiud” (or Abihud) is mostly unknown. He represents the quiet continuation of the royal line during the Persian period, when the Jews lived under foreign rule with no Davidic king on the throne. His name means “my father is majesty” or “father of majesty/honor.” “Eliakim” also has no detailed story (this is not the same Eliakim as the official who served under King Hezekiah centuries earlier). His name means “God raises up” or “God will establish/raise”. “Azor” means “helper” or “one who helps”. Like the others, he lived during the “silent years” between the Old & New Testaments, when Israel was under Persian, then Greek, then Roman influence.

14.x: There are no details about “Azor,” “Zadok” (Sadoc), “Achim” (Akim), or “Eliud” in Scripture. This section shows that God preserved the royal line of David through many generations of ordinary, unknown people, not just through famous kings or leaders like David, Solomon, or Zerubbabel.

15.x: “Eliud,” “Eleazar” & “Matthan” have no Biblical stories. These names still fall in the relatively obscure period between the return from Babylonian exile and the birth of Jesus (roughly covering the last 150-200 years before Christ under Greek & then Roman rule). Matthew continues to compress the list to maintain his structure of exactly 14 generations in this section. Eleazar was a very common name in Israel (there are several Eleazars in the OT, including Aaron’s son & a famous priest). However, this particular Eleazar is only mentioned here.

16.x: Matthew says the father of “Joseph” was “Jacob.” Luke 3:23 says it was “Heli.” These are some of the possible ways to harmonize the two lists: (1) Jacob was also named Heli (as Matthew is also called Levi, or Paul is also called Saul, etc), (2) Matthew gives Joseph’s legal/royal genealogy (through Solomon’s line). Luke gives the physical/biological line (Mary’s line that came from David’s son Nathan, rather than Solomon), since it was not typical in Jewish genealogies to name women, Luke lists Joseph as the son-in-law of Heli (Mary’s father). Luke traces all the way back to Adam, emphasizing Jesus as the Son of Man for all humanity, not just for a royal line. (3) Levirate marriage (an ancient custom from Deut 25:5-6). If a man died without children, his brother would marry the widow so the firstborn son could carry on the dead brother’s name & inheritance. According to an early tradition (“Epistle to Aristides”) recorded by Julius Africanus (~200AD), Jacob & Heli were half-brothers (same mother, different fathers). Heli died childless, so Jacob married Heli’s widow & fathered Joseph, making Joseph the biological son of Jacob (Matthew), but the legal son of Heli (Luke) under the law. Matthew is writing for a Jewish audience, so it’s important for him to prioritize the claim to the Davidic kingdom. Luke’s genealogy is for a broader, often Gentile audience, so it focuses more on Jesus as the Son of Man - tracing a more human/physical line all the way to Adam.

17.x: Matthew organizes his genealogy in a structured, artistic way of 14 in order to make a theological point. David’s name in Hebrew adds up to 14(called gematria - where letters have numerical values): Hebrew: דָּוִד (Dalet = 4, Vav/Waw = 6, Dalet = 4) → 4 + 6 + 4 = 14. By using three groups of 14, Matthew is repeatedly highlighting that Jesus is the Son of David, the promised King from David’s line.

18.x: The betrothal period (called kiddushin) was a formal stage of engagement in ancient Jewish society. It wasn’t just “dating” or casual promise, it was a legally & socially binding agreement to marry. The couple was considered husband & wife in status. Breaking it required a formal divorce. However, they did not live together. Betrothals were often arranged by families rather than chosen purely by the couple. Parents negotiated the match. A bride price might be agreed upon. Love could grow later, but the union was initially more about family alliances & stability. After the betrothal, there was a waiting period before the wedding ceremony. During this time the groom prepared a home (or a place in his family’s house) while the bride stayed with her family. The couple typically did not have sexual relations. This period tested commitment & ensured everything was properly arranged. Even though they didn’t live together yet, faithfulness was required. Infidelity during betrothal could be treated as adultery, which would require the death penalty under the Law of Moses (Deut 22:23-24). The betrothal ended with a wedding ceremony, after which the bride moved into the husband’s household, the marriage was fully consummated, and the celebrations could last several days. Mary “was found with child of the Holy Ghost”, hence the Holy Spirit is literally the Father of baby Jesus. The Father is “Holy” (John 17:11) & the Father is “Spirit” (Jn 4:24), hence “Holy Spirit.” Holy Spirit simply refers to the natural state of God as a Spiritual being in action, while “Father” refers to His relationship to humanity as their creator.

In the Oneness of God, the Holy Spirit, literally the one God, is the Father of the human Jesus. It was the Spirit who “begot” (gennaō) the Son in Mt 1:20. God provided the other half of the generic material, making the man Jesus the ultimate instrument for God to redeem us to Himself. Since God has no flesh or bones (Jn 4:24), He made Himself a body in which to dwell to come into Earth & pay for our sins as the Just God that He is. “God (Holy Spirit) was IN Christ (the human), reconciling the world unto Himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). “For in him (the human Jesus) dwelleth ALL the fullness of the Godhead bodily. And ye are COMPLETE in him, which is the head of ALL principality and power” (Col 2:9-10 KJV). Jesus is not part of the Godhead as Trinitarians teach, rather the entire Godhead is in Jesus. We are COMPLETE with Jesus, because the one God, the Father, fully dwells in him without losing His omnipresence. We don’t need anything else, we don’t need other divine persons or saints or Mary, or anything else. Do not let “your minds be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (2 Cor 11:3 BSB). Jesus is all we need. “Jesus” is the name ABOVE EVERY NAME (Phil 2:9), and it is the ONLY NAME given to men for salvation (Acts 4:12). The entire Bible is about Jesus, culminating in the Revelation of Jesus as the Alpha and Omega, the First and the Last, the Almighty God (Rev 4:8; 22:12-13,16; Isa 9:6). Jesus was “full of the Holy Spirit (God)” (Lk 4:1 BSB). He has access to the divine Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB) as the only begotten of the Father. His body is the temple of the divine Spirit (Jn 2:19). It was at this moment that the human Son was “begotten” (Heb 1:5), “made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal 4:4 KJV). Notice the Son is not “eternally begotten”, that is unbiblical and it’s an Oxymoron (contradictory words paired together), as you cannot be both “begotten” & “eternal”. The Son had a beginning in Mary’s womb after conception by the Holy Spirit: “Thou art my Son, THIS DAY(not eternally back) have I begotten thee…I WILL(future tense) be to him a Father, and he SHALL(future tense) be to me a Son” (Heb 1:5 KJV). On the other hand, since Trinitarians teach that God-the-Father is Jesus’ Father & not the Holy Spirit, they believe that the Holy Spirit simply overshadows Mary to prepare Jesus’ body for God-the-Son (who is the 2nd divine person of the Trinity): “but a body hast thou prepared me” (Heb 10:5 KJV) - this text cites Psalms 40:6-8, where David is praying to YHWH. For Oneness, YHWH is one divine person who came & incarnated in the human Jesus. For Trinitarians, YHWH is the divine essence that is fully shared among the three divine persons of the Trinity, so “YHWH” could mean either “God-the-Father”, “God-the-Son”, or “God-the-Spirit”. In this case, they say this YHWH refers to the Holy Spirit since He was the one who came to prepare the body for God-the-Son. Then God-the-Father “sends” God-the-Son into the world to indwell baby Jesus. Here we find a crucial difference between Oneness & Trinitarians. For a Trinitarian, it was only God-the-Son who came into the world and incarnated baby Jesus. For a Oneness, it was God-the-Father, the only true God (Jn 17:3), who came Himself into the world & indwelt His human Son to redeem humanity to Himself (2 Cor 5:19). God so loved the world that He came Himself to redeem us to Himself, otherwise God wouldn’t be really all loving. For what kind of love is it when you send someone else to die & you get all the credit? The “sending” of the Son does not refer to “sending a pre-existent Son into the world”, rather it simply means “sending the human Son from the womb out into the world”, just like how John the Baptist was also “sent from God” (Jn 1:6, 33). Being “sent” does not mean being pre-existent in Biblical language.

19.x: Joseph could have accused Mary and had her stoned for infidelity, but being a “righteous” person, he chose mercy. Mercy is higher than justice: "mercy triumphs over judgement” (James 2:13 LSB). God desires “mercy, and not sacrifice” (Mt 9:13 KJV). For “if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses” (Mt 6:14-15 KJV). Being able to forgive is a salvation issue. Thankfully for Joseph, Mary was innocent, however, his true character as a man of God shone in such a situation.

20.x: “The angel of the Lord” corresponds to the “angel of YHWH” in the Hebrew Scriptures. Over time, Jewish attitudes toward the divine name developed significantly. Out of reverence for the command not to take God’s name in vain (Exo 20:7), and from Hellenistic (Greek) cultural influence, many Jews eventually became afraid to even utter the name of YHWH. In ancient Israel (prior to the 5th century BC), the name of YHWH was spoken openly in prayers, blessings, and everyday religious life. This is reflected throughout the OT. For example: “then began men to call upon the name of the LORD(YHWH)” (Gen 4:26 KJV); Abraham “called upon the name of the LORD(YHWH)” (Gen 12:8 KJV); “Then called I upon the name of the LORD(YHWH); O LORD(YHWH), I beseech thee, deliver my soul.” (Ps 116:4 KJV); and “whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD(YHWH) shall be delivered” (Joel 2:32 KJV). After the conquests of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BC, Jewish society came under strong Greek cultural influence. Greek philosophers had already begun to question the morality of their traditional gods, who were often portrayed as impulsive, immoral, and excessively human. For example, the Titan Cronus (Saturn) was told that one of his children would overthrow him, so he swallowed each of them at birth. Likewise, Zeus was notorious for infidelity, while his wife Hera often directed her anger toward Zeus’ victims rather than toward him (like when the nymph Echo distracted Hera so Zeus could escape, Hera cursed her to only repeat the last words spoken to her). Many such myths depict violence, deceit, and immorality. To address these concerns, Greek philosophers began reinterpreting their traditions. By the 5th century BC, Theagenes of Rhegium pioneered allegorical interpretation, explaining myths as symbolic representations of natural forces or moral truths rather than literal events. This approach was later developed further by Stoicism (3rd–1st centuries BC), which taught that the many gods were expressions of a single divine principle known as the Logos: the rational structure governing the universe (it was never a person for the Greeks, the personhood of the Logos was later developed by Christian philosophers like Justin Martyr in ~150AC who would later become the foundation of Trinitarianism). In this allegorical view, Zeus represented the active rational principle (“Logos” or the “Word”), while other gods symbolized different aspects of nature or manifestations of this Logos. For example: Zeus was the active rational principle, the soul of the universe, the cause of life; Hera was the air, Poseidon the water, Athena intelligence, etc. This philosophical shift developed gradually between the 6th and 4th centuries BC through thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle. By the 3rd century AC, it reached its climax in the thought of Plotinus, who described ultimate reality as “the One,” a transcendent, ineffable (something too great, intense, or sacred that CANNOT BE NAMED or described in words) source beyond all being, language, and comprehension. These philosophical developments formed part of the broader intellectual environment in which Jewish people lived. Add to this the increasing Jewish reverence for the divine name, and it quickly resulted in Jews completely avoiding pronouncing “YHWH” directly. This is reflected in the Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures produced in Alexandria between approximately 250 and 130 BC. In this translation, any Bible verse that portrayed YHWH as a nameable, personal God, or as doing something unworthy of a Supreme God (like walking or feeling emotions) was modified (for example, compared the LXX rendering of these verses: Ex 3:14; Hosea 11:9; Amos 9:6; Deut 32:8; Genesis 2:4;3:8,9; Ps 23:1, etc). So now, instead of being stoned to death for BLASPHEMING the name of YHWH (Lev 24:16), you could now get stoned for simply NAMING the name of YHWH. This is how the LXX renders Lev 24:16: “And he that NAMES the name of the Lord, let him die the death: let all the congregation of Israel stone him with stones; whether he be a stranger or a native, let him die for NAMING the name of the Lord” (Lev 24:16, The Orthodox Study Bible based on the LXX). Hence, by the time the NT writers came about, instead of writing “YHWH,” they’d use the impersonal Greek “Kyrios” (Lord) instead. Therefore, when reading the NT, it is important to know when “Lord” in the text is specifically referencing the OT YHWH, or if it’s calling Jesus as YHWH incarnated, or simply “Lord”, as a more general title. Early Christian philosophers like Justin Martyr would also be influenced by the Supreme God of the Greeks. This led some Christians to begin to see God-the-Father as the same ineffable God of the Greeks. This is why Trinitarians today still do not know the name of the Father: because He is the same Supreme God of the Greeks who cannot be named: “For no one can utter the name of the ineffable God;and if anyone dares to say that there is a name, he raves with a hopeless madness” (Justin Martyr, First Apology 61, ~150AC). Oneness Christians do know that the name of the Father is “Jesus” (YHWH-Saves) (Isa 9:6; Mt 1:21; Heb 1:4;2:12; Phil 2:9-11; Jn 5:43; 10:25; 17:6, 26; Rev 22:3-4; also see Jn 17:11,12; Rev 14:1 in texts based on the CT or the MT [the TR follows a minority variant]), that’s why ALL biblical baptisms were done explicitly in the name of Jesus (Acts 2:38; 8:12,16; 10:48; 19:5; 22:16; Rom 6:3-4; 1 Cor 1:13-14; Gal 3:27; Col 2:12; Js 2:7), which is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:12) because it is the name above every name (Phil 2:9). *** Matthew 1:20 also states that Jesus was “conceived” (literally “begotten”) by the Holy Spirit. This connects directly to the Oneness of God, where the Father & the Holy Spirit as the same divine person, not distinct persons of the Godhead. John 4:24 states that “God is Spirit,” where “God” means Father, Holy Spirit, YHWH, or the divine Spirit of Jesus. The Bible is clear that there is only one Spirit, not multiple divine spirits. Ephesians 4:4 states: “There is one body and one Spirit,” and 1 Corinthians 12:13 teaches that all believers are united by that same one Spirit. Yet, Scripture uses many different titles for this one Spirit: (1) Spirit of God (Gen 1:2), (2) Spirit of YHWH (Isa 11:2), (3) Holy Spirit (Ps 51:11), (4) Spirit of the Father (Mt 10:20), (5) Spirit of Christ (Rom 8:9; 1 Pet 1:11), (6) Spirit of Jesus (where it’s literally being used interchangeably with Holy Spirit [Acts 16:6-7 CT]), (7) Spirit of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:19), (8) Spirit of the Lord (Lk 4:18), (9) Spirit of the Living God (2 Cor 3:3), (10) the Spirit (Eph 4:4; 1 Cor 12:11), (11) Spirit of Truth (Jn 14:17), (12) Spirit of Grace (Heb 10:29), and (13) the Eternal Spirit (Heb 9:14). These are not different spirits or separate divine persons within the Godhead, but different titles and descriptions of the same one divine Spirit who is God.

21.x: “Jesus” is a modern transliteration of the Greek name Iēsous (the book of Joshua in the LXX is called Iēsous as well, which matches the fact that both Iēsous’ will lead the people to the promised land), which itself is a translation of the Hebrew name Yeshua or Yehoshua. The Hebrew name Yehoshua (translated as “Joshua” in the OT) is a combination of two distinct parts: (1) Yeho-: prefix derived from YHWH, (2) -shua: from the Hebrew root word yasha, which means “to save” , “to deliver”, or “to rescue”. When put together, the name literally translates to “YHWH is salvation” or “YHWH saves”. The name was not random. Neither Mary nor Joseph chose the name. The angel of YHWH gave specific instructions to name the baby “Jesus” because His name identifies His purpose as the embodiment of God’s saving power, literally, the human person through whom “YHWH saves”. Paul states this reality in 2 Cor 5:19: “God(YHWH) was IN Christ reconciling the world unto HIMSELF(not THEMselves)” (KJV). This name was prophesied since the OT: “Therefore my people shall know my name(Jesus): therefore they shall know in that day that I am He that doth speak” (Isa 52:6 KJV) & “the LORD(YHWH) shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one LORD(YHWH), and His name one(YHWH-Saves, aka Jesus)” (Zech 14:9 KJV) - notice how God constantly tells us that He is One and not Three, if “one” in this verse meant “one as a unity,” then the “one” name would also have to be a “unity” of names, and it’s not: “One” LORD means exactly that, ONE. The human Messiah INHERITED (Heb 1:4) the NAME THAT IS ABOVE EVERY NAME (Phil 2:9-11) from the Father (YHWH). Jesus (YHWH-saves), is the ONLY NAME under heaven given to men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:10,12). Therefore, “Jesus” is the name of the Father inherited to His Son(human Messiah), and He is present wherever He places His name: “For in Him dwelleth ALL the fullness of the GODHEAD bodily, and ye are COMPLETE in Him, which is the HEAD of all principality and power” (Col 2:9-10 KJV). Jesus is not “part of the Godhead”. The entire Godhead is in Jesus. The name of YHWH represents the presence of YHWH Himself. Recall in the OT how YHWH said He would put His name on the temple: “I have hallowed this house, which thou has built, TO PUT MY NAME there for ever..” (1 Kings 9:3 KJV), and then we see that YHWH was physically present in the temple: “the glory of the LORD had filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11 KJV). Likewise, in the NT, that temple is the body of Jesus (“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” [Jn 2:19 KJV]), which was indwelt by the divine Spirit of the LORD (Col 2:9-10), fulfilling the types and shadows of the OT.

22-23.x: Matthew cites Isaiah 7:14 as being fulfilled here, with Jesus being: “God with us,” from Emmanuel (Immanu El): ʿimmānû (עִמָּנוּ): “with us” (from the preposition ʿim meaning “with,” plus the suffix -ānû for “us”) & ʾēl (אֵל): “God” (a common Hebrew word for God, as in El Shaddai or El Elyon). This “God” refers to the entire Godhead (Col 2:9-10), to the same YHWH of the OT come in the flesh. It does not refer to a 2nd divine person of the Trinity, but to the one God manifested in the flesh (1 Tim 3:16). God is Spirit (Jn 4:24). He(YHWH) does not have flesh & bones, so He made Himself a body to come to Earth & to redeem us to Himself (2 Cor 5:19). The Father IS NOT the Son, rather the Father IS IN the Son. When Trinitarians mock Oneness as having a schizophrenic Jesus talking to himself, they misunderstand the definition of Oneness. Oneness refers to the one DIVINE person, which does not include the human. The human is the temple of the one divine person(Jn 2:19). “I and my Father are one” (Jn 10:30 KJV). If the Father was the Son, then Jesus would have said: “I am the Father”, yet there is more than the Father in Jesus, it is the union between the divine Spirit & the sinless man: (1)Father & (2)Son. The word for “one” used in Jn 10:30 is “hen”, the neuter form of “one” in Greek, meaning “one as a unity”, a unity between “the only true God(the Father), and Jesus Chris(the human Son)” (Jn 17:3 KJV). If the Father & the Son were the same person, it would have used the Greek word for “one” as “heis”: singular masculine one. This is also why we see Jesus submitting his human will to the Divine Will of the Father (Lk 22:42). The human is useless without the divine Spirit (Jn 5:19,30), so when Jesus prays to the Father, the authentic human is praying to the divine Spirit for strength. By coming into our world, God made Himself a body in which to dwell, but as an authentic human being, Jesus had to play by human rules, and besides eating, drinking, sleeping, and hurting, the man Jesus ALSO needed Spiritual strength from the Father (like the rest of us) to gain the strength necessary to carry out his mission. What DOES NOT make sense, is the Trinitarian view, where a God prays to another God, much less if they’re supposed to be the same God as two divine persons within the Godhead talking to each other. Trinitarianism defies math, logic, Scripture, common sense, any logical reasoning & the supposed co-equality within the persons of the Godhead. That is why, when asked about HOW the Trinity works, they’ll answer with: “it’s a mystery you have to accept,” and then cite you Deut 29:29: “The secret things belong unto the Lord our God” (KJV). Also, by definition, a God is the one prayed to, not the one doing the praying, as there is nothing or anyone above God. The “mystery” IS NOT how a Trinity works, the “mystery” is HOW the one God came to manifest in the flesh: “And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory” (1 Tim 3:16 KJV).

24-25.x: Bibles based on the Textus Receptus (KJV, NKJV, MEV, Reina-Valera) & Majority Text (WEB, MSB), have the word “firstborn” to describe Jesus in v. 25. 98.6% of available manuscripts contain “firstborn” (percentages from “The Text-Critical English NT Byzantine Text Version,” Robert Adam Boyd). However, the two oldest mss found: Vaticanus & Sinaiticus from Alexandria (Egypt), do not have the word “firstborn” (only 0.5% of available manuscripts do not have the word “firstborn”). This led many scholars to assume that the word was added later by some scribe, hence, modern Bible translations based on the Critical Text (NIV, NASB, ESV, etc) omit it. This could or could not be true, as Vaticanus & Sinaiticus also have many other errors in them, but even if it were true, and “firstborn” was added to this verse, in Luke 2:7, Luke describes Jesus as “firstborn’. So if it was added to Matthew, it was not a corruption, rather, someone probably knew Jesus was the “firstborn” from Luke and decided to include that true information in the book of Matthew as well. Jesus has to be the firstborn in order to be the heir to the Davidic Kingdom through Joseph. This means that Jesus’ brothers (Mt 13:55-56; Mk 6:3; Mt 12:46-50; Mk 3:31-35; Lk 8:19-21; Jn 2:12; Jn 7:3-10; Acts 1:14; Gal 1:19; 1 Cor 9:5; 1 Cor 15:7) cannot be from a previous marriage of Joseph, rather they’re younger brothers that were born to Mary after Jesus was born. “And knew her not til”: in the Bible, the word “know” or “knew” is frequently used as a euphemism for sexual intercourse. This comes from the Hebrew word “yada”, which literally means “to know” in the sense of intimate, personal, or experiential knowledge - but in specific contexts, it clearly refers to sexual relations. We see examples of this in Gen 4:1: “Adan KNEW Eve his wife; and she conceived” (KJV); Gen 4:17: “Cain KNEW his wife; and she conceived” (KJV), etc. Isaiah 7:14 prophesied that Jesus would be born of a virgin, so Matthew clarifies to his Jewish audience that Mary did not have sex with Joseph UNTIL Jesus was born. In Catholic dogma you MUST believe that Mary is a perpetual virgin under threat of potential condemnation (if fully aware of the teaching and willfully reject it). Councils like the Lateran Council of 649AC, fully affirmed this belief in explicit & systematic terms. It is not an optional doctrine, it is considered part of the deposit of faith. Their Catechism teaches that: “The deepening of faith in the virginal motherhood led the Church to confess Mary’s real and perpetual virginity EVEN IN THE ACT OF GIVING BIRTH… In fact, Christ’s birth DID NOT DIMINISH HIS MOTHER’S VIRGINAL INTEGRITY but sanctified it” (CCC 499) - meaning that, from a Catholic standpoint, Jesus’ birth was twice as miraculous: (1) Mary got pregnant as a virgin, and (2) Jesus somehow teleported out of Mary’s womb in order to maintain Mary’s “virginal integrity”. The first fake gospel that tried to argue for Mary’s virginity said that a great light shone in the cave so that their eyes could not bear it: “And in a little that light gradually decreased, until the infant APPEARED, and went and took the breast from His mother Mary” (Ch 19, Protoevangelium of James, ~150AC). Due to this dogmatic belief, most Catholic Bibles in Latin America completely remove the Greek word “heos” (until) from their translations. These include Bibila Torrest Amat (1828), Biblia Straubinger (1951), Latinoamerica (1972), Biblia de America (1999), Biblia de Navarra (2008), and Biblia de Jerusalen Latinoamerica (2020). The one I know that actually keeps the word “until” is the Bible used by their theologians: the original Biblia de Jerusalen (1997). In English, due to Protestant pressure in the US, Catholic Bibles tend to be more honest since the Vatican II council of 1965, when they began to translate from the original languages rather than the Latin. When English-speaking Catholics deal with the word “until”, they argue that it does not imply that anything changed afterward. Hence, they say that in Biblical language, the word “until” often marks what happens up to a point without saying what happens afterward, and they give 2 Samuel 6:23 as an example: “Michal… had no child UNTO(until) the day of her death” (KJV). Since Michal did not have a child AFTER death, that implies that Mary did not have sex after giving birth to Jesus. This, of course, is a mockery of rational thought. Context obviously determines whether there will be a change afterward or not. Of course Michal did not have children AFTER death, because she was dead. But if the text had said: “Michal had no child UNTIL she turned 30” any reasonable person would know that she, in fact, had children AFTER she turned 30. Likewise, if I said: “I was a virgin UNTIL marriage”. Any reasonable person would know I had sex AFTER marriage. But if I said: “My grandfather was loyal UNTIL death”. Any reasonable person would know my grandfather didn’t become disloyal AFTER death, since that is physically impossible. The bottom line is that Matthew 1:25 strongly implies that she had sex after Jesus was born. Jesus is called the FIRSTborn (Lk 2:7), as opposed to the LATERborn brothers & sisters mentioned elsewhere in Scripture (Mt 13:55-56; Mk 6:3; Gal 1:19), otherwise “only son” would be expected. Mt 1:24 says “Joseph… took unto him his wife” (KJV). Marriage in Jewish context includes sexual union as normal & expected. There is no indication Joseph & Mary had a permanent abstinent marriage. If Mary did not give herself to Joseph, she would have sinned and disobeyed the apostle Paul’s teachings for spouses of not depriving each one (1 Cor 7:3-5). There is no Biblical statement saying that Mary & Joseph were exempt. John 7:5 says that “neither did his brethren believe in him..” (KJV), which implies that in a normal family, the expectation is that brothers trust each other, hence, a normal household dynamic. Mt 12:47 says “thy mother and thy brethren stand without(with-out, as opposed to with-in, it’s an archaic word that means ‘outside’)” (KJV), where mother & brothers are mentioned together, suggesting a standard nuclear family structure. Also, Acts 1:13-14 clearly distinguishes Jesus’ brothers from his disciples. They also try to argue that “brothers” does not strictly mean biological brothers, but that it could mean “cousin” or “relative”. However, Luke specifically uses the Greek word for “relative (sungenēs)” (Lk 1:36 BSB) & Paul uses the Greek word for “cousin (anepsios)” (Col 4:10 BSB), yet they both differentiate between “relative” and “cousin” and specifically call Jesus’ brothers “adelphoi” (biological brothers) (Gal 1:19; 1 Cor 9:5; Lk 8:19-20; Acts 1:14, etc). If Biblical evidence is not enough, even extra-biblical evidence calls James “the brother of Jesus” (Josephus, a Jewish historian in his "Antiquities of the Jews,” 20.9.1, ~93AC). Others try to argue that James is the son of “the other Mary” (Mt 27:61), but the “other Mary” was the mother of “James the less” (Mk 15:40; Mt 27:56), not “James the Just”, who is typically identified as the brother of Jesus. Every time a family member of Jesus is mentioned, he is mentioned in relation to Jesus. For example: “Mary THE MOTHER OF JESUS”, or “HIS(Jesus’) brothers James, Joseph…” or “James, THE LORD’S BROTHER”. But every time other James are mentioned, they are mentioned in relation to other people, like “James OF ALPHEUS”, “James THE LESS”, “James OF ZEBEDEE (James the Great)”, “James THE BROTHER OF JOHN”, “Mary the MOTHER OF JAMES (as opposed to ‘Mary the MOTHER OF JESUS’)”, etc. Also, in the 12 apostles, you have two who are named James: James the Great, and James the Less. However, James,THE BROTHER OF JESUS, did not believe in Him(Jn 7:5; Mk 6:3) & was not part of Jesus’ followers until after Jesus appeared to him after his resurrection (1 Cor 15:7). Finally, since James was Jesus’ biological half-brother, many early Jewish Christians (Ebionites) saw him as the universal bishop with the utmost apostolic authority (like how Catholics see the Pope today). This is why some of the earliest apocryphal gospels are written in James’ name, in order to usurp his authority as leader of the Jerusalem Church. We can see his leadership in the NT: (1) he has the last word in the first Church council of Acts 15:13,19; (2) Paul reports to James in Acts 21:18-19; (3) he is singled out along with Peter in Gal 1:18-19; (4) Peter reports to James in Acts 12:16-17; (5) he is listed first in some lists that even include Peter like Gal 2:9 or Acts 21:18, where he is singled out as the primary figure. Also, Eusebius of Caesarea explicitly calls James the first bishop of the church at Jerusalem, and cited earlier traditions including Clement of Alexandria, who says that after Jesus' ascension, Peter, James, and John chose James THE JUST as bishop of Jerusalem. The second-century writer Hegesippus describes James as having “succeeded to the government of the Church in conjunction with the apostles” and says that he was universally known as “the Just.” The Protoevangelium of James (~150AC) tries to argue for Mary’s perpetual virginity, although it is full of contradictions (like displaying Mary’s parents as wealthy, while Scripture shows that Mary was poor in Lk 2:24 & Lev 12:8) and exaggerated stories (like angels hand-feeding Mary, or the midwife’s hand withering for questioning Mary’s virginity) that not even Catholics take it as Scripture. Another argument used is Jesus leaving His mother to John instead of his biological brothers, but this can be explained by: (1) His brothers were not present at his crucifixion, only John & the women (Mt 27:55-56; Jn 19:25-27); (2) Jesus’ Spiritual Family is above his biological family (Lk 8:20-21), and (3) at the time of the Crucifixion, James still did not believe in Jesus (Jn 7:5; Mk 6:3; 1 Cor 15:7). Finally, they may try to fall back onto the “Church Fathers” for support. First, they are not “Church Fathers”, as the Church existed way before any of them, that is the technical term given to them to try to give them authority. Second, history is selective, the works of anyone they considered a “heretic” were burned. Third, they all contradict each other, find one arguing for Mary’s virginity, and I can find others who would deny it (the same can be done about any topic). Finally, although many of them did believe in Mary’s perpetual virginity, they did not have any evidence, rather they relied on faulty arguments like: “that body of hers which was appointed to minister to the Word… might not know intercourse with a man after the Holy Spirit came into her and power from on high overshadowed her. And I think.. that just as Jesus was the first-fruit among men of the purity that consists in chastity, so was Mary among women” (Origen, ~245AC), and that’s it, that’s all the evidence they had - essentially arguing that sex with Joseph would be adultery against the Holy Spirit, or that just as Jesus was a virgin, so must have been his mother as well. As time went on, they began to come up with other arguments, like Jerome(~383AC) saying it is unthinkable for Joseph to have relations with Mary after such a miraculous birth, Joseph would not defile the "temple of God"; or Ambrose of Milan (~390AC) saying Mary was a consecrated vessel uniquely set apart for God, and that Ezekiel's closed gate (Eze 44:1-2) is a figure of Mary and her perpetual virginity; Christ passes through it without opening it, and Joseph does not open it, etc. Never blindly follow what others believed in, even if they’re the majority, rather inquire as to the evidence that they had in order to reach such conclusions.
